questions.question: What is the difference between a Docker image and a Docker container?
questions.title: Docker Image vs Container — Key Difference
questions.direct_answer: A Docker image is a read-only blueprint (like a class in Java); a Docker container is a running instance of that image (like an object) — you can run many containers from one image.

interviewer_intent.testing: Foundational Docker concept — asked in almost every Docker interview question
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating image and container as the same thing
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Use the class/object analogy — shows you can map new concepts to things you already know

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The analogy I use is class and object in Java. A Docker image is like a class — it's a blueprint, a template, a read-only definition. The image contains the file system layers with the application, dependencies, and configuration. By itself, it doesn't do anything. A Docker container is like an object — it's a running instance created from that image. When I run 'docker run myapp', Docker takes the image and starts a container from it. The container is live: it has a running process, writable file system, network connections. I can create multiple containers from the same image — just like I can create multiple objects from the same class. All three containers run independently from the same blueprint. The image is immutable — I never modify it once built. If I need to change the application, I build a new image and run new containers from it. Containers are ephemeral by default — when I stop and remove a container, any changes made inside it are lost because they were in the container's writable layer, not the image. For persistent data, I need Docker volumes.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Image: read-only blueprint (like a Java class) — defines the environment
Container: running instance of an image (like a Java object)
One image → many containers running simultaneously
Images are immutable — you build a new one, you don't modify a running one
Containers are ephemeral — data inside is lost unless you use volumes

followup_questions: What are Docker volumes and why are they needed?
What is a Docker layer and how does it relate to images?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app image run as multiple containers
speakable_v2.hook: The image-container confusion trips up almost every beginner — the class-object analogy from Java makes it click instantly.

groups.heading: Docker image
groups.text: A read-only blueprint. It's built from a Dockerfile, stored on disk as stacked layers, and never modified after creation. Think of it as a Java class definition.

groups.heading: Docker container
groups.text: A running instance created from an image. It has an active process, a writable layer on top of the image, and its own network. Think of it as an object instantiated from that class.

beats.text: You push images to registries and version them. You run containers in your environments. Deploying a new version means building a new image and replacing the running containers — you never patch a live container.

speakable_v2.cap: non-obvious: containers are ephemeral by default. Any files written inside a container disappear when the container is removed. If you need persistence, that's what Docker volumes are for.

questions.question: What are Docker image layers and how does layer caching work?
questions.title: Docker Image Layers and Layer Caching
questions.direct_answer: Docker images are built as stacked layers — each Dockerfile instruction adds one layer — and if a layer hasn't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached layer, making builds much faster.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical Dockerfile optimization knowledge — shows you've written real Dockerfiles
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing about layer caching and writing Dockerfiles in a way that always invalidates the cache
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the optimization: copy pom.xml and download dependencies first, then copy source code — so dependency layer is cached across most builds

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Every instruction in a Dockerfile — FROM, COPY, RUN, ENV — creates a new layer in the image. Layers are stacked on top of each other to form the final image. Each layer represents a filesystem change. Layer caching is a significant build optimization. When I build an image, Docker checks each layer: if the instruction and its inputs haven't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached layer instead of rebuilding it. This can turn a 5-minute build into a 10-second build. The key rule is that once a layer is invalidated — because its instruction or input changed — all subsequent layers are also rebuilt. This matters a lot for how you order instructions. A common mistake in Java Dockerfiles is copying all source files early. When you change any Java file, all the subsequent layers get rebuilt — including the 'RUN mvn install' that downloads all Maven dependencies, which takes minutes. The optimization is to split the copy into two steps: first copy pom.xml only and run 'mvn dependency:go-offline' to download all dependencies. That becomes one layer. Then copy the source code and compile. Now, if you only change Java source files, only the last layer rebuilds — the dependencies layer is still cached from last time.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Each Dockerfile instruction creates one immutable layer
Docker caches layers — if input unchanged, reuse cached layer
Cache invalidation: when a layer changes, all layers after it rebuild too
Optimization: copy pom.xml first, download deps, then copy source — deps layer stays cached
Order matters: put frequently-changing files in later layers

followup_questions: What is a multi-stage Docker build and why is it used for Java?
How do you inspect the layers of a Docker image?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Every line in your Dockerfile creates a layer — and the order you write those lines determines whether your builds take 10 seconds or 5 minutes.

beats.text: Docker images are built as a stack of layers. Each instruction in a Dockerfile — FROM, COPY, RUN — adds one immutable layer on top of the previous ones. The final image is all those layers combined.

Layer caching is the real payoff. If a layer's instruction and its inputs haven't changed since the last build, Docker reuses the cached version instead of rebuilding it. One changed layer invalidates all layers below it.

For Java, the optimization is to COPY pom.xml first and run Maven dependency download as a separate layer. That dependencies layer gets cached. Then COPY your source code. Now when you change a Java file, only the compile layer rebuilds — the multi-minute dependency download is skipped.
production trap: copying all source files in a single COPY instruction means any file change invalidates the dependency download layer, making every build slow. Split COPY into two steps.

speakable_v2.cap: Put the things that change least at the top of the Dockerfile, and the things that change most — your source code — at the bottom. Cache invalidation flows downward.

questions.question: What do 'docker ps' and 'docker images' show and how are they different?
questions.title: docker ps vs docker images — What They Show
questions.direct_answer: 'docker images' lists all Docker images on your local machine; 'docker ps' lists running containers; 'docker ps -a' shows all containers including stopped ones.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Docker CLI literacy — candidates who can't name these commands have never used Docker
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Mixing up images and containers in these commands
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the fields shown in docker ps: CONTAINER ID, IMAGE, COMMAND, CREATED, STATUS, PORTS, NAMES

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: These two commands address the two core concepts in Docker. 'docker images' shows me all the Docker images that exist on my local machine — the read-only blueprints. It shows the repository name, tag, image ID, when it was created, and the size. Images stay on your machine until you remove them with 'docker rmi'. 'docker ps' shows the currently running containers — the live instances. It shows the container ID, which image it was created from, the command running inside it, how long it's been up, its status, which ports are exposed, and the container's name. If I stop a container, it disappears from 'docker ps'. To see stopped containers too, I use 'docker ps -a' — the '-a' flag means all. Stopped containers still exist and can be restarted or inspected; they just don't appear in the default 'docker ps'. The relationship between the two: I first download or build an image, which appears in 'docker images'. When I run 'docker run myimage', a container is created from that image and appears in 'docker ps'. Multiple containers from the same image all reference the same image entry.

sections.title: Key Points
content: docker images: lists images on the local machine (repository, tag, ID, size)
docker ps: lists running containers only
docker ps -a: lists all containers including stopped ones
A stopped container still exists — use docker ps -a to see it
docker run creates a container from an image; docker start restarts a stopped one

followup_questions: How do you remove stopped containers and unused images?
What does the PORTS column in docker ps show?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Two of the most-used Docker commands show completely different things — and mixing them up tells an interviewer you haven't actually used Docker.

groups.heading: docker images
groups.text: Lists all images on your local machine — the read-only blueprints. Shows repository name, tag, image ID, creation date, and size. Images stay until you remove them with docker rmi.

groups.heading: docker ps
groups.text: Lists currently running containers. Shows container ID, which image it came from, the running command, uptime, status, exposed ports, and name. Stopped containers don't appear here.

items: docker ps: running containers only — add -a to see stopped containers too
docker images: all local images regardless of whether any containers are running
You can have an image with zero running containers, and that's normal

beats.text: After you run docker-compose down, docker ps shows nothing. But docker images still shows all your images — they're on disk, ready to run again.

speakable_v2.cap: sharp edge: docker ps -a reveals stopped containers that are consuming disk space. Run docker system prune to clean up stopped containers, dangling images, and unused networks in one go.
followup_handoff: How do you remove stopped containers and unused images?

questions.question: What does it mean that Docker containers are ephemeral, and how do you persist data?
questions.title: Docker Containers Are Ephemeral — Persisting Data
questions.direct_answer: Ephemeral means container data is lost when the container is removed; persist data using Docker volumes, which are managed storage that survives container lifecycle and can be shared between containers.

interviewer_intent.testing: Critical real-world Docker knowledge — loss of data on container restart is a common gotcha
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Writing to the container filesystem assuming it's persistent — then being surprised when data disappears
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish volumes (Docker-managed) from bind mounts (host directory) — both persist data but in different ways

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: Ephemeral means temporary — each Docker container has its own writable layer on top of the image layers. Any files written inside the container — logs, uploaded files, database files — go into that writable layer. The writable layer lives only as long as the container. When I run 'docker rm' to remove the container, that writable layer is deleted with it. All the data written there is gone. This is by design for stateless applications — a Spring Boot API server doesn't write anything to its local filesystem in normal operation, so ephemeral containers work fine. But for stateful workloads like a MySQL database container, you absolutely need persistence. Docker solves this with volumes. A volume is Docker-managed storage that exists outside the container's lifecycle. I attach a volume to a container when I run it: 'docker run -v mydata:/var/lib/mysql mysql'. Now MySQL writes its data to the volume. If I remove and recreate the container, I reattach the same volume and the data is still there. There are also bind mounts, where I map a specific host directory into the container — 'docker run -v /home/user/data:/app/data myapp'. That's useful for development when I want live code changes to be visible inside the container.

sections.title: Key Points
content: Ephemeral: container's writable layer is deleted when the container is removed
Stateless apps (Spring Boot API): fine without volumes
Stateful apps (MySQL, uploaded files): must use volumes
Volume: Docker-managed storage outside container lifecycle — '-v volumeName:/path'
Bind mount: map a host directory into the container — useful for development

followup_questions: What is the difference between a Docker volume and a bind mount?
How do you back up data in a Docker volume?

speakable_v2.standard_example: MySQL container with a Docker volume for database persistence
speakable_v2.hook: Ephemeral sounds scary but it's actually a feature — until you run a database container without a volume and lose all your data on restart.

beats.text: Every container has a thin writable layer on top of the read-only image. Anything written inside the container — files, logs, database rows — goes into that writable layer. When you remove the container, that layer is deleted. That's what ephemeral means.

For stateless apps like a Spring Boot REST API, this is fine. The app doesn't write anything locally, so ephemeral containers work perfectly. For stateful workloads like a database, you need data to survive container restarts.

items: Docker volume: Docker-managed storage outside the container lifecycle — survives docker rm
Bind mount: maps a specific host directory into the container — useful for dev
Usage: docker run -v mydata:/var/lib/mysql mysql attaches a volume at the database data path

beats.text: gotcha: if you run a MySQL container in local dev without a volume and then run docker-compose down, you lose your entire local database. Always define volumes for stateful services in docker-compose.yml.

speakable_v2.cap: Stateless containers love being ephemeral. Stateful containers need volumes. Knowing the difference is what separates a developer who understands Docker from one who just copies commands.

questions.question: What is the sequence of steps from pulling a Docker image to running a container?
questions.title: Docker Pull to Running Container — The Full Sequence
questions.direct_answer: docker pull fetches the image from a registry; docker run creates a new container from that image and starts it — if the image isn't local, docker run automatically pulls it first.

interviewer_intent.testing: Basic Docker workflow understanding — can you explain what happens when you run a container?
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing that docker run pulls the image automatically if it's not local
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention the intermediate 'docker create' step — docker run actually does create + start in one command

sections.title: How to Answer
sections.content: The full sequence starts before you even have the image. The first time I use an image, I can explicitly run 'docker pull eclipse-temurin:21' to fetch the image from Docker Hub to my local machine. The image is stored in Docker's local image cache. Then 'docker run eclipse-temurin:21' creates a container from that image and starts it immediately. Docker run actually does two things internally: 'docker create' creates the container and sets up its writable layer and configuration, and then 'docker start' starts the process inside it. You can do these separately but 'docker run' combines them for convenience. If I run 'docker run' for an image that isn't in my local cache, Docker automatically does a 'docker pull' first — you don't have to explicitly pull beforehand. After the container is running, 'docker ps' shows it. To stop it: 'docker stop containerName' sends SIGTERM to the main process and waits for graceful shutdown, then SIGKILL if it doesn't stop. The stopped container still exists — 'docker ps -a' shows it. 'docker rm containerName' removes it permanently. 'docker rmi imageName' removes the image from local storage.

sections.title: Key Points
content: docker pull: fetch image from registry to local cache
docker run: creates and starts a container (auto-pulls if image not local)
docker run = docker create + docker start internally
docker stop: graceful shutdown (SIGTERM then SIGKILL)
docker rm: remove stopped container; docker rmi: remove image from local storage

followup_questions: What is the difference between docker stop and docker kill?
How do you run a container in detached mode?

speakable_v2.standard_example: Spring Boot app packaged as a Docker image
speakable_v2.hook: Most people jump straight to docker run — but knowing what actually happens under the hood shows you understand Docker, not just its commands.

items: docker pull: fetches the image from a registry to your local cache
docker run: creates a container from the image and starts it immediately
If the image isn't local, docker run pulls it automatically first
Internally, docker run = docker create + docker start in one step

beats.text: When you first run docker run eclipse-temurin:21 on a fresh machine, Docker checks local cache, finds nothing, pulls the image layers from Docker Hub, then starts the container. Next time it uses the cached image and starts in seconds.

Stopping and cleanup: docker stop sends SIGTERM to the main process for graceful shutdown. After a timeout it sends SIGKILL. Docker rm removes the stopped container. Docker rmi removes the image from local storage.

speakable_v2.cap: candidates miss: a stopped container still exists and takes up disk space. Use docker ps -a to see it, and docker system prune to clean up all stopped containers at once.
followup_handoff: What is the difference between docker stop and docker kill?
